title: What is a binary tree — each node has at most 2 children (left child and right child); the topmost node is called root.

s1_definition.profdef: A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure made of nodes, where each node holds a value and has at most two children referred to as the left child and the right child. The single topmost node is the root, nodes with no children are leaves, and the longest path from the root to a leaf defines the height. Because the branching is limited to two, binary trees are the basis for binary search trees, heaps, and expression trees.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the organisational chart at the National Bank of India. At the very top is the Branch Manager — that is the root. The manager supervises at most two deputies, a left deputy and a right deputy. Each deputy in turn supervises at most two officers below them, and so on down the chart. The officers at the bottom with nobody reporting to them are the leaves. The whole chart is a binary tree because every person oversees at most two direct reports.
s1_definition.oneliner: A binary tree is a hierarchy where every node has at most two children, one left and one right, under a single root.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure made of nodes, where each node holds a value and has at most two children referred to as the left child and the right child. The single topmost node is the root, nodes with no children are leaves, and the longest path from the root to a leaf defines the height. Because the branching is limited to two, binary trees are the basis for binary search trees, heaps, and expression trees.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the organisational chart at the National Bank of India. At the very top is the Branch Manager — that is the root. The manager supervises at most two deputies, a left deputy and a right deputy. Each deputy in turn supervises at most two officers below them, and so on down the chart. The officers at the bottom with nobody reporting to them are the leaves. The whole chart is a binary tree because every person oversees at most two direct reports.

**One line to remember:** A binary tree is a hierarchy where every node has at most two children, one left and one right, under a single root.

sections.s2_technical:
A binary tree node needs three things: a value, a reference to the left child, and a reference to the right child. In Java the node class holds `BigDecimal value`, `Node left`, and `Node right`, where a null child means that branch is absent. The tree itself is usually referenced by its root node.

Several terms matter. The root is the entry point. A parent is any node with children; a child is a node directly below a parent. Leaves have both children null. The depth of a node is its distance from the root, and the height of the tree is the longest root-to-leaf path. A tree is balanced when the left and right subtrees of every node differ in height by at most a small constant, which keeps operations efficient.

Traversal is how we visit every node. Depth-first traversals come in three flavours: inorder visits left subtree, then the node, then right subtree; preorder visits the node first, then left, then right; postorder visits left, right, then the node. Breadth-first traversal visits the tree level by level using a queue. For example, a recursive inorder method is `inorder(node.left); visit(node); inorder(node.right);`.

A senior-level point is that a plain binary tree gives no ordering guarantee, so searching it is linear. The power comes from adding rules. A binary search tree keeps left less than node less than right, giving logarithmic search when balanced. A heap keeps the parent larger or smaller than its children, giving fast access to the maximum or minimum. In banking, trees underpin order books, decision engines, and index structures, so understanding the base binary tree is foundational.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India models its branch approval hierarchy as a tree. The Branch Manager is at the top, and each manager has at most two deputies who each have at most two officers. When a large loan needs sign-off, the request flows through this hierarchy. We need a structure that captures this at-most-two-children shape with a single top. That is precisely a binary tree with a root and left and right children.

Problem 2 — Management wants to list every officer in the hierarchy in a readable order and also count the total number of people and the depth of the chart. Traversing the binary tree lets us visit every node to produce the listing, and a recursive height calculation gives the depth.

In our mini-project we build a `HierarchyNode` with a name, a left child, and a right child, and an `OrgTree` service that performs an inorder traversal to list names, counts the total nodes, and computes the height. The demo builds a small hierarchy rooted at the Branch Manager and logs the traversal, count, and height.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a hierarchy where BranchManager has left Deputy-Rajesh and right Deputy-Priya, and Deputy-Rajesh has left Officer-Anil and right Officer-Bela.

Step 1: We call `inorder(BranchManager)`. Inorder goes left first, so it recurses into Deputy-Rajesh before visiting the manager.

Step 2: Inside Deputy-Rajesh, it again goes left into Officer-Anil. Officer-Anil has no children, so it visits Officer-Anil, then tries the right child which is null and returns.

Step 3: Back in Deputy-Rajesh, the left subtree is done, so it visits Deputy-Rajesh, then recurses right into Officer-Bela, which visits Officer-Bela.

Step 4: The entire left subtree of the manager is now visited, so it visits BranchManager.

Step 5: Finally it recurses right into Deputy-Priya, which has no children, so it visits Deputy-Priya. The inorder sequence is Officer-Anil, Deputy-Rajesh, Officer-Bela, BranchManager, Deputy-Priya.

Step 6: We call `countNodes(BranchManager)`, which recursively adds one for each node and returns five. We call `height(BranchManager)`, which finds the longest path Manager to Deputy-Rajesh to Officer-Anil, giving a height of three levels.

```
[2026-10-26 20:05:01] INFO    Inorder listing of the hierarchy:
[2026-10-26 20:05:01] INFO    Visit: Officer-Anil
[2026-10-26 20:05:01] INFO    Visit: Deputy-Rajesh
[2026-10-26 20:05:01] INFO    Visit: Officer-Bela
[2026-10-26 20:05:01] INFO    Visit: BranchManager
[2026-10-26 20:05:01] INFO    Visit: Deputy-Priya
[2026-10-26 20:05:01] INFO    Total people in hierarchy: 5
[2026-10-26 20:05:01] INFO    Height (levels) of hierarchy: 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure made of nodes, where each node holds a value and has at most two children, a left child and a right child. There is exactly one node at the top called the root, nodes with no children are called leaves, and the longest path from the root down to a leaf is the height of the tree. The defining rule is simply that the branching is limited to two children per node.

The analogy I use from my banking work is the branch approval hierarchy at the National Bank of India. The Branch Manager sits at the root, each manager has at most two deputies, each deputy has at most two officers, and the officers at the bottom with no reports are the leaves. Modelling it as a binary tree let me traverse the whole hierarchy to list everyone, count the total number of people, and compute the depth of the chart, all with simple recursion.

On traversal, I explain the three depth-first orders. Inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. Preorder visits the node first, then left, then right. Postorder visits left, right, then the node. There is also breadth-first traversal, which goes level by level using a queue. In my demo I used inorder to produce a readable listing and recursion to compute the count and the height.

The senior-level point I always make is that a plain binary tree gives no ordering guarantee, so searching it is linear. The real power comes from adding rules on top of the binary shape. A binary search tree enforces left less than node less than right to give logarithmic search when balanced, and a heap enforces a parent-child ordering to give fast access to the minimum or maximum. In banking these structures underpin order books, decision engines, and indexes, which is why understanding the base binary tree first is so important.
